meta.h1: The Winning Paper: what takes an award entry from good to great
meta.byline: 4 October 2026 · Sam · AI researcher, Run with Foxes

intro.p: I've spent this week inside other people's award papers. With a team of AI agents I read 470 of them, each one from start to end. The largest set runs to 1.6 million words, and we read most of it more than once. That made 1,032 full readings and 4.4 million words.

We put the same 51 questions to every paper in the archive, and 16 more to the papers in our main comparison. Does it state an insight? Does it say what would have happened without the campaign? Does it show profit, or only revenue? That gave us 23,902 answers. Where a question called for it, we also copied out the sentence in the paper that the answer rests on, which came to 5,713 passages. We counted 969 objectives and 6,320 charts. And we logged 1,599 separate times that an author named something else that might have caused their own result.
I did all of that because I wanted to know one thing. When two decent pieces of work go in for the same award, why is one awarded and the other isn't?
intro.hl: I did all of that because I wanted to know one thing. When two decent pieces of work go in for the same award, why is one awarded and the other isn't?

intro.p: I thought the answer would be the story. I expected the awarded papers to have the insight and the papers that weren't awarded to be missing it. That isn't what the counts show. Nearly every paper has an insight, a diagnosis and a strategy that follows from it. Those are table stakes. Sales rising while a campaign runs is correlation. What the awarded papers add is evidence of causation: evidence that the work caused the result.

So if you've been asked to write an award entry, this report is for you. It starts with a checklist: what to do, what never to do, and the evidence behind each line. Each chapter after it makes one point, shows the count behind it, and then tells one case that does it well. There are seven: IAG Cargo, IBM, Marie Curie, Direct Line, Lidl, Art Fund and Pancreatic Cancer Action. Two of them sell to businesses. Four spent under a million a year. Two led with television advertising. Use it to take your own entry from good to great.

Of the 470 papers, 389 are from Paul Dervan's own archive, collected over the past 20 years and reaching back to 1980. The other 81 are Irish winners that anyone can open: 40 from the Effie Awards Ireland and 41 from ADFX. We also read the entry rules of 9 award bodies, in their own published guides.

intro.title: What we read
intro.cap: Every paper was read from start to end by an AI agent working to a written list of questions. For the comparison, the agents were not told which papers had been awarded.

intro.p: The comparison at the centre of this report uses 183 of those papers. They come from one long-running effectiveness award, in the five competitions between 2011 and 2018 where the archive holds both sides: 96 papers that were awarded and 87 that were entered and not awarded. Same award, same competitions, same rules.
Anything entered for an award like this is already decent work. So the differences below are differences in how the paper was written.

checklist.title: Your checklist
lead: Sixteen lines. The numbers come from one comparison: 96 papers that were awarded, set against 87 papers that were entered for the same award in the same five competitions and weren't awarded. Each line is something the awarded papers do more often, or something the award bodies ask for in their own guides, or both.

do.t: Start with the table stakes: an insight, a diagnosis and an objective.
do.e: 99% of awarded papers state an insight, and 93% of the papers that weren't awarded. A paper without one stands out for the wrong reason. The IPA's outline asks for objectives in the form "Increase profits/revenue by X% within X year(s)".

do.t: Be able to say your whole case in one sentence.
do.e: The IPA's pack asks you to put it "in one paragraph, or better yet, in one sentence", with one chart that shows it. This line rests on the guide alone.

do.t: Give about half your words to results and proof.
do.e: The IPA allows 4,000 words and says results "should take up about 50% of the paper if not more". By our agents' estimate, the middle awarded paper gives 45%, and the middle paper among those that weren't awarded gives 35%.

do.t: Say what would have happened anyway.
do.e: 83% of awarded papers do this, and 53% of the papers that weren't awarded. This is the counterfactual. The IPA's payback guide builds on it: "Incremental sales value = Actual sales value - Base sales value".

do.t: Lead with what the campaign added.
do.e: 58% of awarded papers state their main result as the incremental part, and 39% of the papers that weren't awarded. The IPA's sum above is the reason: the base is what you'd have sold anyway.

do.t: Name every other cause, and put a figure against each one.
do.e: 78% of awarded papers rule out three or more other causes with a figure, and 45% of the papers that weren't awarded. The IPA's pack says the benefit must be one that "cannot be attributed to other factors such as promotions, pricing, seasonality, distribution increases, underlying market growth, competitor weakness".

do.t: Show a number at each step from the work to the sale.
do.e: 95% of awarded papers do this, and 68% of the papers that weren't awarded. The IPA's outline asks "Why it happened? (linking it to the activity)".

do.t: Come back to your diagnosis and show that it changed.
do.e: 92% of awarded papers do this, and 80% of the papers that weren't awarded. This line rests on our counts alone.

do.t: Show three years or more of your measure.
do.e: 82% of awarded papers do this, and 56% of the papers that weren't awarded. The IPA's outline asks for the brand's situation "going back several years". Report at least a year of results after the work began too: 78% of awarded papers do, and 61% of the papers that weren't awarded.

do.t: State the payback as profit, with the margin and the sum.
do.e: 69% of awarded papers make a profit claim, and 41% of the papers that weren't awarded. The IPA's payback guide says to "prove that the activity paid for itself and generated a net profit".

do.t: Put a source on every figure.
do.e: Figures with no source appear in 9% of awarded papers and 37% of the papers that weren't awarded. The Effie entry kit says "All data included in the entry form must reference a specific, verifiable source."

Nearly every paper does. Compared like for like, 87% of awarded papers admit a limit or something that did not work, and 88% of the papers that weren't awarded. An Effie jury tip puts it this way: "You'll gain credibility by being honest about all the factors that created success."

never.t: Never offer a sales rise as proof.
never.e: A rise while the campaign ran is correlation. 42% of awarded papers lead with the total rise, and 61% of the papers that weren't awarded. The IPA's pack lists the other factors a rise can come from.

never.t: Never report revenue as your return on investment.
never.e: 19% of awarded papers give revenue only, and 33% of the papers that weren't awarded. The IPA's payback guide asks for net profit.
No awarded paper did. 14% of the papers that weren't awarded did. The IPA's payback guide asks you to prove the activity paid for itself.

never.t: Never compare only with the last six months.
never.e: 2 awarded papers do this, and 7 of the papers that weren't awarded. The numbers are small, and this line rests on our counts alone.

close: One caution, and it is the report's own lesson. These counts show what awarded papers do more often. That is correlation too. So where an award body's own guide asks for the same thing, the line quotes it. Where no guide does, the line says it rests on our counts alone.

lede.do: State an insight about people, a diagnosis that names a cause, and an objective with a number in it. Be able to say the whole case in one sentence.
lede.label: Do this

lede.p: Insights matter. So does a diagnosis, and a strategy that follows from it, and a story that runs in order. They matter so much that nearly every paper in the archive has them, awarded or not. That is what table stakes means. You can't sit down without them.
lede.pull: That is what table stakes means. You can't sit down without them.

blocks.p: Figure 1.1 takes five things a well-built paper has and counts them in both groups.

blocks.alt: Bar chart. States an insight: 99% and 93%; States a commercial objective: 89% and 86%; Diagnosis names a cause: 96% and 98%; Says why the strategy answers it: 97% and 98%; Order: problem, strategy, results: 86% and 87%
blocks.title: The table stakes. Nearly every paper has them
blocks.cap: Share of papers. Insight: 95 of 96 awarded, 81 of 87 not awarded. Commercial objective: 85 of 96 awarded, 75 of 87 not awarded. A diagnosis that names a cause: 92 of 96 awarded, 85 of 87 not awarded. Says why the strategy answers it: 93 of 96 awarded, 85 of 87 not awarded. Order runs problem, strategy, results: 83 of 96 awarded, 76 of 87 not awarded.

blocks.p: Read that chart the right way round. It doesn't say these things are unimportant. It says they are so important that almost nobody enters without them. Only 1 awarded paper in 96 has no stated insight. If yours is missing one of these, a judge will notice, and it's a flag. So start here, and get them right. Then go on, because having them puts you level with everyone else. The rest of this report is about what takes a paper from there to great.

Two more things belong here, and both come from the IPA's own guide. One is an objective with a number in it. The guide gives the pattern: "Increase profits/revenue by X% within X year(s) of the campaign". LowLow's 2014 ADFX paper does it for each product line, with targets such as "Bring New Consumers to the Category: Target 30,000", and then reports against each one. The other is being able to say the whole case in a sentence. Chapter 6 comes back to that.

Since an insight is something you can't enter without, it's worth being sure yours is one. The forms ask for it, and only one award body says what it means. The Effie entry kit asks for "INSIGHTS- not just facts or observations, but what came out from the data points/research". Its jury tips add that a data point isn't an insight, and neither is your objective said again.

So use a test you can apply. Is it about people? Is it about these people and this brand? And did the idea come from it? Here is a paper that passes all three, from a business most of us will never see an ad for.

paras.p: IAG Cargo flies freight in the holds of passenger aircraft. At the start of 2016 it relied on a handful of very large accounts, and it wanted more from its small customers. They are freight forwarders, often firms you could count on the fingers of one hand. The obvious answer was a loyalty scheme: points for tonnage.

Before building one, the team went to meet the customers. They interviewed 15 small forwarders in each of five markets, in offices and warehouses beside airports. The paper is frank about where they started. They had every customer's name, address and account value. “But we knew nothing about them as people.”

What they found is about people. In every firm two people decide. The owner draws up the list of carriers, and a junior clerk picks one from it day to day. Some owners told them they felt bad that they couldn't pay their clerks more. And both deal with a local sales agent they trust more than a faceless organisation in another country.

You can see the scheme coming from that. It rewards the clerks as well as the owners, with fuel cards in the US and movie nights in India. It lets an owner pool the clerks' rewards so the whole team benefits. It lets the sales agents decide who is invited. The points for tonnage stayed. Those three things were added to them, and all three came from the interviews.

Then the paper shows its result the plain way, with no model. It compares members with similar firms that didn't join, grouped by how much they spend. Members' spend rose 18% in the year, 11 percentage points more than the others. The paper puts the extra revenue at €14 million, on a budget of €272,000.

blocks.p: You have 4,000 words and a judge with a pile of papers to get through. The first line matters. Some awarded papers open on a fact you can't ignore. Some open on a question. And Boddingtons, a Gold winner in 1994, opens by telling you the job was hard: “This paper is not easy to write.” You read the next line.

lede.do: Give a figure for what would have happened without the campaign. Lead with what the campaign added. Name every other cause and put a figure against each.
lede.label: Do this

lede.p: Sales went up while the campaign ran. That is correlation. It tells you the two things happened together. It doesn't tell you the campaign caused the rise, because a price cut, wider distribution, good weather or a rival's bad year could have done the same. Showing causation is the widest difference in everything we read. It is also an old worry. The John Smith's Bitter paper that won the Grand Prix in 1982 put the limit of its own argument in one line: “Causal relationships can only be inferred, never demonstrated.”
lede.pull: Sales went up while the campaign ran. That is correlation.

blocks.p: Figure 2.1 takes five ways a paper can show causation. For each one it gives the share of awarded papers that do it and the share of the papers that weren't awarded. Look at the gap between the two groups in each row. Three of the five are the widest gaps in the report.

blocks.alt: Bar chart. A figure for what would have happened anyway: 83% and 53%; Headline is what the activity added: 58% and 39%; A model or a control test: 81% and 46%; Rules out 3+ other causes with a figure: 78% and 45%; A number at each step, work to sale: 95% and 68%
blocks.title: Awarded papers say what would have happened without the work
blocks.cap: Share of papers. Gives a figure for what would have happened anyway: 80 of 96 awarded, 46 of 87 not awarded. Headline result is what the activity added, not the total rise: 56 of 96 awarded, 34 of 87 not awarded. Uses a model or a control test: 78 of 96 awarded, 40 of 87 not awarded. Rules out three or more other causes with a figure: 75 of 96 awarded, 39 of 87 not awarded. Shows each step from the work to the sale with a number: 91 of 96 awarded, 59 of 87 not awarded.

blocks.p: Nearly half of the papers that weren't awarded never say what sales would have been without the activity. That figure has a name, the counterfactual, and it is the plainest test of causation there is. More than half of those papers lead with the total rise and credit the campaign for all of it. The awarded papers lead with the incremental part, which is what the campaign added.
You don't need a model to do this. Here is a paper that had none. For one part of its result, it found its counterfactual on a map.

paras.p: In February 2011 an IBM computer called Watson played the American quiz show Jeopardy! against the two finest players the game had seen, and won. IBM sells to businesses. Nobody watching was going to buy a Watson. The campaign around the show was there to bring in the people who do buy from IBM, and the paper counts $254 million of booked revenue from leads that came in through Watson events and materials.

For that figure the paper doesn't estimate what IBM would have won anyway. It raises the question itself, calls it a valid one, and says it isn't how IBM judges a campaign. Where it does ask what the campaign added, it is careful. Sales of the servers Watson ran on had been in long decline, and after the show they were up 9.1%. Only $76 million of that could be tracked to a Watson lead. How much of the rest did the campaign cause?

The paper looks for a place like North America that saw far less of the campaign. It picks Western Europe, where IBM did no Watson marketing and the show wasn't televised, though the news travelled. Server sales in the two regions tracked closely beforehand. Take the tracked $76 million out of North America's 9.1%, and 5.8% is left to explain. Europe grew 7.5%, or 2.9% once the falling euro is taken out. The difference between the 5.8% and the 2.9%, about $68 million, is what the campaign might have added.

And then it does something I didn't expect. It calls that figure a ceiling. “It's an upper limit as other factors in which W. Europe and NA differed will be involved”, it says. It leaves the whole $68 million out of its return, because the exact size is unclear. The return it does claim, at least 2.4 times the spend in profit, is worked out on the tracked revenue alone.

Any team can do what this paper does with its server sales. Find the nearest thing you have to your market without your campaign. Show that the two moved together before. Take out what else differs. Then claim the gap, or less.

blocks.p: Across the 389 archive papers, the authors named another possible cause of their own result 1,599 times. They named price, promotions, distribution, the market, competitors, the season, the weather and product changes. In 1,023 of those they answered with a figure, a chart or a named source. In 576 they answered with a sentence.
Figure 2.2 shows how those answers divide. Look at how many were given a figure, and how many only a sentence.

blocks.alt: Bar chart. Answered with a figure, a chart or a source: 1023; Answered with a sentence: 576
blocks.title: Of 1,599 other causes named, 1,023 were answered with a figure
blocks.cap: All 389 archive papers. Each time an author named another possible cause of the result, the agent recorded whether the paper answered it with a figure, a chart or a named source, or with words only.

blocks.p: Figure 2.3 takes the middle paper in each group. It shows how many other causes that paper names, and how many it rules out with data. Look at the second pair.

blocks.alt: Bar chart. Other causes named: 6.0 and 4; Ruled out with data: 4.0 and 2
blocks.title: The middle awarded paper names 6 other causes and rules out 4 with data
blocks.cap: The middle paper in each group, which is the median. Awarded: 6 named, 4 ruled out with data. Not awarded: 4 named, 2 ruled out with data. 96 awarded papers and 87 not awarded.

blocks.p: Most teams already hold the data to close that gap. This one had no tracking research, and closed it anyway.

paras.p: Marie Curie gives free nursing care to people who are terminally ill. Its Great Daffodil Appeal runs every March, and just over a quarter of the money comes from volunteers with collecting tins. In 2010 the charity tried something it had never done. Most charity advertising asks people to give money. This campaign, mostly on radio, asked people to give an hour and collect it. The whole thing cost £184,151, which the paper says was the smallest budget entered for the IPA's small budget prize up to then.

Collectors went from 13,774 to over 20,000. Then the paper has to show that the advertising did it, and it starts with what it doesn't have. “Due to the low investment in the campaign, we do not have any tracking research at our disposal.”

It has other evidence, and it gives that first. New recruits rose most in the regions where the radio weight was heaviest. And every new recruit signed up through the advertised phone number, Facebook or the web address, where collectors normally register with their local branch. Any small team can do both of those: count sign-ups by the route they came in, and set them against where the advertising ran.

Then comes a list. The paper names six other things that could have brought the collectors in, and answers each one. The usual recruitment by local fundraisers hadn't changed. The main appeal advertising ran in March, and collectors had to register by the end of February. Its rivals outspent it: the two larger cancer charities had 79% and 13% of the advertising in those two months, and Marie Curie had 8%. It had no reason to think cancer deaths had risen. Nobody well known had died of cancer in those weeks. And the weather: March 2010 was colder, less sunny and equally wet, so a fine month didn't bring the collectors out.
One of those answers came from the Met Office.

It is as careful with the return. Collector numbers were already rising a little each year, so the paper works its return out three ways: against the year before, against the five-year average, and against a trend line fitted to the five years before. That gives £2.75, £3.01 and £2.45 for every £1. It uses the £2.45, the most conservative, from there on.

blocks.p: The same habit turns up in the public Irish papers. The Gathering's 2014 ADFX paper asks whether the weather was behind its result, and answers with a date: people had registered, on average, 4 to 6 months before the good weather arrived.

subs.title: What you can still fix, and what you can't

blocks.p: Two rows in Figure 2.1 are decided long before anyone writes. If nobody built an econometric model and no region was held back as a control, no paragraph can supply one. Say so early and plainly. Then build the best comparison you have. That could be a forecast made before the activity, the market, a close rival, or a period or a place without the work.

The other three are within any writer's reach. Put a figure against each other cause. State what the activity added and not the total. Show the number at each step: people saw it, it changed what they thought or did, and sales moved.

lede.do: Write your diagnosis in one sentence. Then show, in your results, that the thing you diagnosed has changed.
lede.label: Do this

lede.p: Here is where the story itself goes from good to great. Every paper starts well. The great ones come back to where they started.
lede.pull: Every paper starts well. The great ones come back to where they started.

subs.title: Did the thing you diagnosed change?

blocks.p: Figure 3.1 puts two things side by side. The first is whether a paper says what was wrong. The second is whether its results show that same thing changing. Look at how close the two groups are on the first, and how they part on the second.

blocks.alt: Bar chart. States a diagnosis that names a cause: 96% and 98%; Results show the diagnosed problem changed: 92% and 80%
blocks.title: Nearly every paper makes a diagnosis. Awarded papers return to it
blocks.cap: Share of papers. States a diagnosis that names a cause: 92 of 96 awarded, 85 of 87 not awarded. The results show that the diagnosed problem changed: 88 of 96 awarded, 70 of 87 not awarded.

blocks.p: The usual gap looks like this. A paper says the problem was how people saw the brand. Then its results report sales. Sales may well have risen. But the paper said the cause was a belief, so a judge will want to see the belief move.
Direct Line's 2016 paper is the one to read for this.

paras.p: Direct Line made its name in 1985 by cutting out the middle-man. By 2014 price comparison sites had put the middle-man back, and Direct Line's quotes and sales were falling year after year.

The paper could have stopped there and called it a technology problem. It says so itself, and it doesn't. Its diagnosis is about what people thought of the brand: “We had gone from the consumer champion known for 'cutting out the middle-man' to an undifferentiated brand in a deeply distrusted industry”. And it puts a number on undifferentiated. Asked which insurer they would prefer if price were equal, people scored Direct Line and several of its rivals between 10% and 12%.

The strategy follows from that. Be the insurer that fixes the problem. The company changed what it did first, with a promise to fix your car in seven days or pay you £10 a day, and repairs finished within seven days went from 35% to 70%. Then it hired Winston Wolf, the fixer from Pulp Fiction, to say so.

Now look at what the results measure. They report quotes and sales, as you'd expect. But they also go back to the number in the diagnosis. Preference for its car insurance rose from 11.3% to 13.8%. After one year Direct Line scored 15% and the second brand 12%. The two statements the strategy was built on, being easy to deal with and taking care of your insurance so you can get on with your life, improved by 13% and 22%.
The thing it said was broken is the thing it shows mended. That is the loop.

blocks.p: The test takes two minutes. Write your diagnosis in one sentence. Then find the chart in your results that shows that exact thing changing. If it isn't there, find it, or say that you couldn't measure it.

blocks.held: Paul's own account of what a strong story does, from judging: diagnosis, to strategy, to results.
blocks.label: Held for Paul

lede.do: Show your measure over three years or more. Compare against a baseline such as a forecast or a control. Report at least a year of results.
lede.label: Do this

lede.p: A result measured against last year tells a judge little, because last year might have been a bad one. A line that runs back several years shows whether this is a real change or an ordinary wobble.
lede.pull: A line that runs back several years shows whether this is a real change or an ordinary wobble.

blocks.p: Vodafone's 2018 ADFX paper is at the long end. It estimates what it added from April 2013 to June 2017, about four years.
Lidl's 2018 paper shows what a long line does for a claim.

paras.p: Lidl opened its first UK store in 1994. For twenty years it spent its whole budget on short-term deals and offers. From 2014 it moved to national advertising, to take on one belief: you get what you pay for, so cheaper must be worse.
The paper was written four years later, and its first chart runs from 1994 to the end of 2017. So before it claims anything, you can see the whole line.

That matters, because Lidl was already growing. A paper that set 2017 against 2013 could have claimed the lot. This one tells you sales grew 9.5% a year from 2009 to 2013, and 15.5% a year from 2014 to 2017. So you can see the growth that was already there.

Then it uses a model to divide that growth between the advertising, the new stores and everything else. Sales grew by £2.56 billion between 2013 and 2017, and the model gives advertising 24.5% of it. The paper says so near the top: “We will show that advertising is responsible for a quarter of Lidl's sales growth.” A quarter, from a brand that could have pointed at the chart and claimed all of it.

A line that starts long before the work, the growth rate from before it, four years after it, and a baseline from a model. That is each of the stronger rows in this chapter's first chart, in one paper.

blocks.p: I'd like to tell you that five years of history is the mark of an awarded paper. I can't. 26 of 96 awarded papers show five years or more before the activity, and so do 23 of the 87 that weren't awarded. The middle paper in both groups shows three. What separates them is showing a long line at all, and comparing against a baseline such as a forecast or a control.

blocks.held: Paul's view, from judging, that a comparison over five years is stronger than one over six months or a year. The papers support the direction. They can't prove the five.
blocks.label: Held for Paul

lede.do: State the payback as profit. Say what margin you used, take the cost of the activity off, and show the sum. Put a source on every figure.
lede.label: Do this

lede.p: Revenue isn't profit. A return worked out on revenue isn't a return on investment. It's the oldest note in the judges' guides, and it still separates the papers.

blocks.p: Figure 5.1 sorts the papers by how they report payback. The first two are profit. The third is revenue on its own. The last is no payback at all. Look at the last one first.

blocks.alt: Bar chart. Makes a profit claim: 69% and 41%; Shows net profit with the sum: 41% and 23%; Gives a revenue return only: 19% and 33%; Gives no payback at all: 0% and 14%
blocks.title: No awarded paper left payback out
blocks.cap: Share of papers. Makes a profit claim: 66 of 96 awarded, 36 of 87 not awarded. Shows net profit with the sum: 39 of 96 awarded, 20 of 87 not awarded. Gives a revenue return only: 18 of 96 awarded, 29 of 87 not awarded. Gives no payback at all: 0 of 96 awarded, 12 of 87 not awarded.

blocks.p: This is what it looks like when a paper shows its sum.

tags: about £605,000 a year from 2012, no television

paras.p: Art Fund is a charity that helps museums and galleries buy works of art. By 2010 its membership had stalled at around 80,000 and was ageing. So it stopped selling the cause and sold what members get, free or reduced entry to galleries and museums, as a card called the National Art Pass. From 2012 its media budget averaged about £605,000 a year. With no budget for television, over 70% of the marketing money went on press and posters. By 2015 new memberships were 174% higher than in 2010.

The paper has no econometric model, and says so. What it has is a sum you can follow. It names its base: the 5,547 new members who joined in 2010, the year before the launch. It counts only the members above that number in each year. It multiplies them by the average lifetime profit each member brings. That gives £12.9m.

Then it heads off the usual mistake. “Note that this is pure profit rather than revenue, as the cost of all forms of marketing has already been removed from the member contribution figures.” So the £12.9m is what is left after the marketing is paid for. Against a total media cost of £3,166,285, that is £4.07 for every £1 spent.
The base is the paper's own choice, and you could argue for a different one. Every step is on the page, so you can.

blocks.p: If your margin is confidential, say so and say what you used. Lidl's paper, the case in chapter 4, says Lidl doesn't reveal its margins even to its agencies, uses an industry-standard gross margin of 25%, and sets the sum out in three lines. Both the IPA and the Effies also let you show confidential figures as an index.

Charities have no profit margin, and the careful ones find the sum anyway. Marie Curie, the case in chapter 2, counts the 66p in every £1 that goes directly to helping the terminally ill, and treats that as its profit.

subs.title: Payback in the public Irish papers

blocks.p: In the public Irish papers, payback stated as profit is rare. Of 41 ADFX papers, 6 state payback as profit. Of 40 Effie Ireland winners, about 8 or 9 claim a return and none states profit.

subs.title: Put a source on every figure

blocks.p: Result figures with no source appear in 9 of the 96 awarded papers and 32 of the 87 that weren't awarded. Compared like for like, the gap holds: 9% and 26%. The Effie rules disqualify unsourced data. It's the cheapest thing in this report to fix.

chapters.title: Read the scoring before you write

lede.do: Count the points before you count your words. Give the most words to the part with the most points.
lede.label: Do this

lede.p: Much of what's above is in the entry guides, if you read them as a judge would. Count the points before you count your words.
lede.pull: Count the points before you count your words.

blocks.p: Figure 6.1 sets out how four award bodies score an entry, in the words of their own guides. Look at which part of the entry gets the most points in each one.

blocks.title: In the effectiveness awards that publish weights, results get the most points
blocks.cap: From each body's own published guide. We read 94 entry questions and judging criteria across 9 bodies. ADFX is not in the table: its published guides date from 2014 to 2018.

blocks.p: The IPA's pack says the results section "should take up about 50% of the paper if not more". It says you should be able to put the whole argument "in one paragraph, or better yet, in one sentence", with one chart that shows it.
Figure 6.2 shows how much of a paper goes on results and proof, for the middle paper in each group. Set it against the IPA's half.

blocks.alt: Bar chart. Share of words on results and proof: 45% and 35%
blocks.title: The middle awarded paper gives 45% of its words to results and proof
blocks.cap: Share of the paper's words in the sections on results, proof, other causes and payback, for the middle paper in each group (the median). Each share is the agent's estimate from the paper's sections. Awarded: 45%. Not awarded: 35%. The IPA's pack asks for about 50% or more.

blocks.p: 35 of 96 awarded papers give half or more, against 16 of 87. Compared like for like, that gap narrows to 32% against 24%, so take it as a pointer. The IPA's own line is the firmer ground.

chapters.title: What the best papers teach about thinking

lede.do: Claim what you can prove, and say plainly what you can't.
lede.label: Do this

lede.p: This is the chapter I didn't plan. I expected the strongest papers to claim the most. They claim less, and then they make it stick. We asked the agents to write one line on what each paper teaches about clear thinking. That gave me 389 lines. I read all of them, and the same habits kept coming back.
lede.pull: They claim less, and then they make it stick.

lede.p: They rule out the other causes one at a time, each with its own answer.

They say what they can't prove, and narrow the claim to what they can. This habit isn't a difference between the two groups. Compared like for like, 87% of awarded papers admit a limit, and 88% of the papers that weren't awarded. It's what careful papers do, whatever the result. One charity campaigned for a change in the law, and the law passed. Its paper says the law would have passed eventually anyway, and claims only that the campaign helped it happen sooner. One car launch had no model, so its paper worked out how little of the sales rise the campaign would need to account for to cover its costs. Neither paper was awarded.
The paper that says it most openly had the smallest budget of the seven cases told here.

paras.p: Pancreatic Cancer Action is a small charity, set up by one of the 3% of people who survive the disease beyond five years. Its job is to make the symptoms known, because this cancer is almost always diagnosed too late. Its entire marketing budget was £78,000. It spent £15,000 on a press ad in which three real patients said they wished they had a more survivable form of the disease, and £63,000 on posters in 25 London Underground stations that set out the symptoms.

A paper with that little behind it could have kept quiet about what it lacked. This one says it near the top, under a heading that calls it a disclaimer. “This is not a typical IPA entry paper - we don't have an econometric model or reams of data to demonstrate that our campaign (and not the media budget) was responsible for the effect.”

Then it sets out what it can show. A survey found that 27% of UK adults recognised the campaign. Of those who did, 43% said they knew more about the symptoms than 6 months before, against 16% of people who didn't remember seeing it. The paper asks whether anything else could have caused that, names a television storyline and the death of a well-known actor in the weeks before, and answers in a sentence.

Its return is a projection, and the paper calls it one. It builds what it calls an assumptive model from the published results of earlier cancer campaigns, and it says "let's assume" twice in the working. It takes one of the earlier figures out, because the figure looked like an outlier and leaving it in might have biased the result in the paper's favour. Its top figure is a return of 10,243%. It ends on a floor, which is its own worst case divided by 2.

It won Gold. I can't tell you the disclaimer is why, and this is not a paper that proves its return. What it does is label its guesses as guesses, so you can see which of its numbers were counted and which were assumed. A paper with £78,000 and no model can still do that.

lede.p: They set the targets first and report against each one, including the ones they missed.

They find a fair comparison. BT held one television region quiet. ONLY compared the styles it featured with the ones it didn't. Nissan set its Irish launch against the same car's launch in other countries. Costa counted the same 250 stores throughout, so new openings couldn't flatter the number.

They separate the real problem from the brief. They show the routes that failed, and what each one changed. They build their sums to be cautious: Mercedes-Benz uses the lowest figure for its calculation, and Marie Curie works its return out three ways and keeps the most conservative.

None of this needs a bigger budget. It's a way of thinking about your own work. A team that can write down what was wrong, why this was the answer, what would have happened anyway and what it paid back understands its work better than a team that can't. That's true whether or not the paper is ever entered. I think it's the best reason to write one.

lede.held: Paul on what he has learned from reading brilliant cases: their clarity of thinking and their rigour, in his own words. And what the papers can't show: what he saw in the judging room.
lede.label: Held for Paul

method.t: 389 award papers from Paul Dervan's archive, 1980 to 2024, 342 of them from 2006 on. They are what one person collected over the years, not every paper entered. 40 Effie Awards Ireland winners from the 2021 and 2023 case study booklets, and 41 ADFX papers from 2012 to 2018, are public and were read in full.

Each paper was read from start to end by an AI agent working to a written list of questions: 32 questions on how the paper is built and proved, 16 on diagnosis, cause and time frames, and 19 on the strategy. That made 1,032 full readings and 23,902 recorded answers. Where a question called for it the agent copied out the sentence the answer rests on, 5,713 passages in all, so those answers can be checked against the paper. The share of words on results is the agent's estimate from the paper's sections.

For the comparison, the prize was taken off each paper before it was read. At least 11 papers still name their own prize in their opening lines, and a few have an editor's comment, so the agent was not blind on those. The third pass, on strategy, was not blind and is not used in the comparison.

In each of the first two passes, 32 papers were read a second time by a different agent working on its own. On every count used in this report the two agents agreed on 27 to 32 of the 32. One question was dropped because the agents took it two ways. Separately, two agents each judged the 40 public Effie Ireland winners against the Effie's definition of an insight, and agreed on 30.

96 awarded and 87 not awarded papers from the same award, in the five competitions from 2011 to 2018 where the archive holds both. Seven awarded papers from 2010 were read and left out, because the archive has no paper from that year that wasn't awarded. "Not awarded" is the label on the file; some may have been shortlisted.

Awarded papers are edited before they're printed, so we ran every difference again on papers in the same printed form: the 78 awarded and 50 not awarded papers that have numbered figures. The differences in this report hold there. A model or control test: 82% and 50%. A figure for what would have happened anyway: 87% and 64%. Three or more other causes ruled out with a figure: 78% and 50%. A number at each step: 96% and 74%. A profit claim: 72% and 48%. A trend over three years: 86% and 60%. Unsourced figures: 9% and 26%. Two differences narrow to nine points there: coming back to the diagnosis (91% and 82%), and giving a revenue return only (19% and 28%). Two things did not hold and are not offered as differences: admitting a limit (87% and 88%), and giving half the paper or more to results (32% and 24%).

The agents read each paper's text and not its chart images, so the counts are of what a paper says in words. A target that sits only in a table or chart is not counted, and we report no count of objectives with a target number.

Every quotation in this report was checked word for word against the paper it comes from. Dashes inside a quotation are shown as hyphens. Seven cases are told in full. Each was read from the paper itself, and every figure in a telling comes from a sentence in that paper. They were chosen to show the point of their chapter and to be a mix: two sell to businesses, four spent under a million a year with the figure in the paper, and two led with television advertising. The archive is mostly consumer brands: the agents filed 5 of its 389 papers as business-to-business. The Irish papers are public and linked. The others are published award papers, named by brand, award, prize and year. No author or judge is named.

Percentages are rounded to the nearest whole number. Where a chart prints a gap in points, it is the difference between the two rounded percentages, so it matches what you see on the chart. Worked out from the counts, four of those gaps would be one point different.
It shows what awarded papers contain. It doesn't show that any one of these things wins an award. Brands with the budget for a model may also have had the stronger work.

We've also read every paper for the problem the brand had and the move it made, by category. That map needs a second read before we publish a number from it. And we're building a coach that works through all of this with a writer, one question at a time.
